extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students and math enthusiasts (readers of expository mathematics)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of short expository mathematics write-ups aimed roughly at undergraduate level, each essay presenting motivations, proofs, and examples on a focused topic (often kept brief and occasionally informal).

rubrics_metrics.name: State intended audience / level
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually, the intended audience is me as an undergraduate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear for whom the exposition is written (e.g., undergraduate level). This helps set expectations for background and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose provisional status and invite feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: They are in various stages of (in)completion, and are surely riddled with errors -- so read with a dash of salt! And if you find any errors or have suggestions, please get in touch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about incompleteness or likely errors and provide contact/errata channels so readers can report problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the goal/purpose of the essay
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary goal of this essay is to motivate Cauchy-Schwarz, prove it, and provide a few examples of applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by explicitly stating what the essay intends to achieve (motivate a concept, prove a theorem, illustrate techniques, survey a method, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate concepts and proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: The purpose of this essay is to try to motivate these concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide intuition and motivation rather than only formal statements; explain why the topic matters and how one might be led to the results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep proofs concise / proofs kept to a minimum
rubrics_metrics.description: This is a relatively brief introduction to Fourier analysis... Proofs are kept to a minimum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor brevity where appropriate: present succinct proofs or sketches, focusing on clarity rather than exhaustive technical detail when the aim is exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide self-contained expositions when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: In this essay I give self-contained proofs of both of these.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When feasible, include proofs and arguments that do not require the reader to chase many external prerequisites; if external results are used, either sketch them or provide references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use elementary / accessible methods when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Arnold invented a remarkably elementary proof... his proof doesn't require any Galois theory (nor any group theory!).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer elementary or low-prerequisite approaches to broaden accessibility, highlighting when more advanced machinery is deliberately avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include illustrative examples and applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary goal of this essay is to motivate Cauchy-Schwarz, prove it, and provide a few examples of applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate key ideas via concrete examples and applications to help readers internalize abstract results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give multiple proofs / present variants
rubrics_metrics.description: Here I give two particularly short and striking proofs... Both of these proofs have nice generalizations, which I also discuss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When helpful, present alternate proofs or perspectives to show different techniques and generalizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: State prerequisites and assumptions clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: If you happen to be familiar with the basic properties of Gauss sums, and decide to try to prove Quadratic Reciprocity using these... here's one approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly list the background knowledge the reader should have (or optional prerequisites) so they can decide whether to proceed or review prior material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage active engagement (try before reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: I strongly urge you to try it yourself before reading!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt readers to attempt problems or proofs themselves before consulting the exposition to deepen understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide references and links to original sources
rubrics_metrics.description: There's nothing original in this essay--everything proved is a special case of what appears in the Wigdersons' manuscript -- and my hope is that the relative brevity... will serve as motivation to read the Wigdersons' original paper, which covers a lot more ground and is beautifully written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite primary sources, manuscripts, videos, or surveys and link to them so interested readers can follow up for more depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch background proofs when relying on standard results
rubrics_metrics.description: The proof relies on Euler's famous characterization of graphs admitting an Euler tour; for completeness, we sketch a proof of this as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an exposition uses a standard but nontrivial result, provide at least a sketch to keep the essay self-contained and accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide memorable heuristics / mnemonics
rubrics_metrics.description: I also share a mnemonic that helped me remember the inequality; as a bonus, the mnemonic inspires a version of Holder's inequality that I find much more natural than the usual formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer heuristics, mnemonics, or intuitive rules to help readers remember and apply key results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be concrete and focused in aims
rubrics_metrics.description: My hope is that the relative brevity and the concreteness of my aims will serve as motivation to read the Wigdersons' original paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep essays focused on a clear, concrete aim rather than attempting overly broad surveys in short pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge contributors and influences
rubrics_metrics.description: I'm grateful to David Eppstein for posting this proof... I'm grateful to Boaz Katz for posting this lovely video which introduced me to Arnold's proof; I strongly urge you to watch it both before and after reading my essay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give credit to people and resources that contributed ideas, feedback, or inspiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use expository style appropriate to the chosen audience
rubrics_metrics.description: There are a lot of mathematics I don't understand. When I do understand something, and am feeling particularly excited about it, I write it up. Usually, the intended audience is me as an undergraduate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt tone, level of rigor, and stylistic choices matching the target readers (e.g., informal conversational tone for undergraduates; more formal for advanced readers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include motivating historical or conceptual context
rubrics_metrics.description: Gauss famously proved the existence of a primitive root mod p... In the 1850s, Chebyshev proved several fundamental results about the distribution of primes...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Situate results in historical or conceptual context to increase reader appreciation and understanding of significance.
